title: Prowers County well depth and drilling costs
meta_description: Prowers County wells have a median depth of 100 ft and a median yield of 38 gpm. Here’s what that means for drilling and buying land on the plains.
h1: Water wells in Prowers County, Colorado
intro_html:
Prowers County is classic eastern Colorado plains: a mix of domestic, stock, and big irrigation wells spread around Lamar, Holly, Wiley, Granada, and Hartman. Well logs here are detailed enough to give you a realistic idea of how deep you might drill, how much water to expect, and what it will cost.

The numbers below come from every permitted well in the county with reported depth, yield, and water level. Use them as a planning tool before you buy or build.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Prowers County
sections.html:
Across Prowers County, reported wells have a median total depth of about 100 feet. The middle half run 45 to 300 feet, and the deepest well on record goes down 3,900 feet, so there is a wide spread depending on use and location.

About 49% of wells are shallower than 100 feet, 26% are 100–300 feet, 19% are 300–600 feet, and 6% go past 600 feet. Domestic and stock wells tend to be on the shallower end, while large irrigation wells are often deeper in the plains sediments or fractured bedrock aquifers listed on permits.

When you ask for drilling bids, most contractors will assume a depth range that matches neighboring wells and then price a per-foot add-on if they have to chase water deeper.

sections.heading: Well yield: generally strong production
sections.html:
Yields in Prowers County are usually good. The median reported pump test is 38 gallons per minute. The middle half of wells span roughly 15 to 800 gpm, which reflects the number of big irrigation wells here as well as smaller domestic and stock wells.

Only about 1% of tested wells fall in the 1–5 gpm range, 23% produce 5–15 gpm, and 76% report more than 15 gpm. There are no reported wells under 1 gpm in the available test data.

For a household, anything at or above about 5 gpm is typically workable with proper storage and plumbing. Irrigation and stock operations lean on the higher-yield end, often tapping the unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, the Dakota, or the Southern High Plains aquifer.

sections.heading: Water table behavior and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels, where reported, have a median of 72 feet below ground, with the middle half between about 13 and 188 feet. That tells you the water table can be quite shallow in some spots and much deeper in others, depending on local geology and pumping.

By decade, the median depth to water was about 69 feet in the 1960s, then much shallower at 23 feet in the 2010s, and then deeper at 156 feet in the 2020s. That swing suggests recent measurements are, on average, hitting deeper water levels, which can reflect heavier pumping, drier periods, or simply different types of wells being measured.

Before drilling or buying, compare nearby well logs to see how water levels behave right around your parcel.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling and how the well pattern changed
sections.html:
Prowers County has 3,837 wells in state records, with 2,062 noted as constructed and 2,359 reporting depth. Permitting picked up over time: 95 permits in the 1950s, 246 in the 1960s, 374 in the 1970s, and 210 in the 1980s.

Activity stayed strong with 470 permits in the 1990s and 475 in the 2000s, then eased to 323 in the 2010s and 133 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit on file is from 2025, so drilling is still active.

Domestic and household wells account for about 21% of uses, stock wells 24%, irrigation 38%, and monitoring wells 14%. Common names on the drilling records include Hoffman (Earl Hoffman), Authorized (Pe, Pg), and Ark Valley Pump & Supply (William Smith Jr.).

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
The ground here is mainly alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Typical drilling rates in that material run around $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out to roughly $3,500–$5,500.

Once you add steel or PVC casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished median-depth well usually lands in the $9,500–$17,500 range. Deeper wells push that higher, especially if you’re going several hundred feet to reach a particular aquifer.

When budgeting a build near Lamar, Holly, Wiley, Granada, or Hartman, it’s smart to plan on the higher end until you’ve seen logs for the closest existing wells.

sections.heading: Risks to check: quality, low spots, and siting
sections.html:
On the quality side, there are 16 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles in this general area. That doesn’t mean your water is bad, but it does mean you should review maps, well logs, and test results before finalizing a purchase.

Low-yield wells are less common in the reported data, but they exist, especially where fractured bedrock is patchy. Always look at nearby yields and static levels, not just depth.

Plan your well and septic layout together. Keep separation distances and future building locations in mind so you don’t box yourself in later with driveways, barns, or corrals.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Prowers County well lot
sections.html:
If the parcel already has a well, pull the permit and log to confirm depth, yield, static level, and the named aquifer. For an older irrigation or stock well being converted to household use, understand any legal and physical limits on pumping and treatment.

On raw ground, use nearby wells in Prowers County as your main guide: most are under 300 feet, and yields are usually strong, but there are outliers in both depth and water level. Get a written drilling proposal that explains per-foot pricing, what happens if you have to go deeper, and what’s included in the completion package.

For larger projects, like new homes or small irrigated operations, talk early with a local water consultant about well permitting and any augmentation or change-of-use issues.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Prowers County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on reported well logs in Prowers County, the median total depth is about 100 feet. Half of the wells fall between roughly 45 and 300 feet deep, and about 49% are shallower than 100 feet. Around 26% run 100–300 feet, 19% are 300–600 feet, and about 6% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest well on record at 3,900 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Prowers County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported yields are generally strong. The median pump-test yield is about 38 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between roughly 15 and 800 gpm. About 1% of wells produce 1–5 gpm, 23% make 5–15 gpm, and 76% report more than 15 gpm. That’s usually plenty for household and stock use, and supports many larger irrigation wells in the county.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Prowers County?
faq.a: In Prowers County’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, typical drilling costs run about $35–$55 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, the borehole alone is roughly $3,500–$5,500. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually falls in the $9,500–$17,500 range, with deeper or higher-capacity wells costing more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Prowers County?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location and depth. In this area there are 16 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, plus 2 historic mine features. That doesn’t automatically make a given well unsafe, but it does mean you should review local maps and have any existing or new well tested by a certified lab before using it for drinking.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Prowers County wells?
faq.a: Reported static water levels show some change over time. Median depth to water was about 69 feet in the 1960s, much shallower at 23 feet in the 2010s, then deeper at 156 feet in the 2020s. That recent shift suggests deeper water levels in the newer measurements, but it also reflects which wells were measured. Always compare static levels from nearby wells to judge conditions on a specific property.
